finding: VC-backed founders with a prior success have ~30% chance of success in the next venture vs ~18% for first-timers and ~20% for previously-failed founders (US VC-backed cos, 1986-2003; success = IPO or IPO filing).
source: Gompers, Kovner, Lerner, Scharfstein, 'Performance Persistence in Entrepreneurship', JFE 2010

finding: Founders with 3+ years prior experience in the same 2-digit industry reach top-0.1% growth outcomes at about twice the rate of founders with none; closer industry match is better. Mean founder age of the top 1-in-1000 growth firms is 45.0 (2.7M founders, US Census data).
source: Azoulay, Jones, Kim, Miranda, 'Age and High-Growth Entrepreneurship', AER: Insights 2020

finding: Among multi-founder US unicorns, 57.8% (796 companies) have at least two founders who worked at the same company before founding; shared university accounts for 33.3%. Implies co-departure clusters from one employer are a formation signal.
source: Ilya Strebulaev, 'The Making of a Unicorn Founder Is Changing' (Stanford Venture Capital Initiative data)

finding: Employer pedigree effects are real but period-specific: PayPal's unicorn-founder odds ratio fell from 12.0 (pre-2016) to 1.7 (post-2016); Google's share of unicorn founders rose from 4.4% to 9.1%; MIT's odds ratio rose 1.9 to 6.3; OpenAI went from zero to 1.8%. Pedigree tables must be time-decayed and refreshed.
source: Ilya Strebulaev, 'The Making of a Unicorn Founder Is Changing'

finding: The most prolific spawners of VC-backed startups are companies that were themselves VC-backed and located in startup hubs; spawning rises as the parent's growth slows. Supports weighting SpaceX/Tesla/Anduril/Palantir-type employers over legacy primes.
source: Gompers, Lerner, Scharfstein, 'Entrepreneurial Spawning', Journal of Finance 2005

finding: In a randomized field experiment (about 17,000 emails to 4,500 AngelList investors), investors responded strongly to founding-team information and not to traction or lead-investor identity; team-based investing was judged a rational strategy.
source: Bernstein, Korteweg, Laws, 'Attracting Early-Stage Investors', Journal of Finance 2017

finding: A DOE SBIR Phase I grant (~$150k) approximately doubles a firm's probability of subsequently receiving VC, with large positive effects on patenting and commercialization; regression discontinuity on 7,436 firms, 1983-2013. Effects strongest for financially constrained (young) firms.
source: Sabrina Howell, 'Financing Innovation: Evidence from R&D Grants', AER 2017

finding: Startups that win their first patent via lenient-examiner assignment show ~55% higher employment growth and ~80% higher sales growth over five years, a 47% higher likelihood of raising VC, and more than double the odds of IPO.
source: Farre-Mensa, Hegde, Ljungqvist, 'What Is a Patent Worth? Evidence from the U.S. Patent Lottery', Journal of Finance 2020

finding: Early-stage startups that engage with open-source communities on GitHub are substantially more likely to raise funding (matched diff-in-diff); effect is larger for novel technologies and weaker when GitHub is used only internally or in crowded markets.
source: Conti, Peukert, Roche, 'Beefing IT Up for Your Investor?', Organization Science 2025

finding: Practitioner evidence: Redpoint analysis of 80 dev-tool companies found median stars of 2,850 at seed and 4,980 at Series A; Runa ROSS Index ranks startups by relative star growth from the 1,000-star mark. Counter-evidence: CMU StarScout found ~4.5M suspected fake stars across ~22.9k repos (3.1M / 15.8k after filtering). Star counts must be de-botted and are weak for hardware companies.
source: Runa Capital ROSS Index; He et al., arXiv:2412.13459

finding: Adding open-web mentions (news and other pages) to structured ecosystem data gave a substantial lift in predicting whether a seed/angel-funded startup raises a Series A within a year.
source: Sharchilev et al., 'Web-based Startup Success Prediction', CIKM 2018

finding: Academic startups raise as much money and patent as much as non-academic ones but have a lower likelihood and hazard of exit (IPO/M&A); 'superstar' academics do better. Research pedigree should score highest when paired with an operator co-founder.
source: Roche, Conti, Rothaermel, 'Different founders, different venture outcomes', Research Policy 2020

finding: Used by every vendor (Harmonic, Specter, Dealroom Signal, CB Insights Mosaic momentum) but no rigorous public study of its predictive power was found in this research pass. Treat as a lagging confirmation signal: it shows up after capital, not before.

An XGBoost screen trained on 77,279 European early-stage companies beat the median VC by 25% and the average VC by 29% in a 111-investor benchmark on identical one-pagers. Screening is automatable; selection of outliers is not shown to be.

VCs that adopt data technologies get better at screening startups similar to past ones and double their investments in the top quartile of backward-similarity, while becoming less likely to back the rare breakthrough companies. Design implication: score novelty explicitly and never rank on similarity-to-past-winners alone.
source: Bonelli, 'Data-driven Investors', Review of Financial Studies 2026
